title: CMOS surprises - Nature Electronics
html:
Unexpected effects are still being discovered in complementary metal–oxide–semiconductor (CMOS) circuits, and the results could have implications for the advance of quantum computing.

The development of silicon-based complementary metal–oxide–semiconductor (CMOS) technology, which is central to modern electronics, can be traced back to the work of Frank Wanlass and Chih-Tang Sah of Fairchild Semiconductor, who in 1963 reported building circuits using complementary n-type and p-type metal–oxide–semiconductor transistors1. Since then, decades of industrial innovation have carefully refined the technology to the point at which billions of transistors are now regularly crammed onto a single chip. But despite their ubiquity, and detailed development, CMOS circuits can still offer up surprises, not least when operated at low temperatures.

Electronics that work at low — or more precisely cryogenic — temperatures can potentially be used to construct energy-efficient computing infrastructure2 and create the control electronics needed to run practical quantum computers3. Previous investigations of circuits operating at such temperatures have uncovered a range of novel phenomena, from quantum dots that can function as nonlinear circuit elements4 to on-chip thermometers based on the emergence of superconductivity in thin films5. Now, writing in this issue of Nature Electronics, Alberto Gomez-Saiz, John Morton, Fernando Gonzalez-Zalba and colleagues show that high-performance superinductors can be created within CMOS circuits using titanium nitride (TiN) thin films native to the manufacturing process.

Superinductors, which are inductors with a characteristic impedance larger than the superconducting resistance quantum (6.45 kΩ), are typically based on complex, purpose-built structures such as Josephson junctions or twisted two-dimensional materials. By contrast, the researchers — who are based at Quantum Motion in London, as well as University College London, Imperial College London, the University of Cambridge, CIC nanoGUNE in San Sebastián, and the Basque Foundation for Science — create their integrated superinductors using the films of TiN, which become superconducting at deep-cryogenic temperatures, found in the poly-resistors of the 22-nm fully depleted silicon-on-insulator process from GlobalFoundries.

Quantum Motion along with companies such as HRL Laboratories (which is now part of IBM), Diraq and Intel are looking to develop quantum computers using semiconductor spin qubits and, in doing so, leverage the tools that underpin conventional computing. The research team at Quantum Motion show that their approach can be used to build radiofrequency single-electron transistors, devices that are widely used as sensors in semiconductor-based quantum computers. The sensors are created, in particular, by co-integrating a resonator containing the superinductor and a silicon quantum dot formed within the same integrated circuit. The resulting system has a footprint of only 18 μm2 and offers a power signal-to-noise ratio of 4,500 in an integration time of 4 ns.

As Thaddeus Ladd of HRL Laboratories notes in an accompanying News & Views article, “the finding that TiN in an unmodified, off-the-shelf CMOS metallization achieves superinductor-grade performance — and without any process engineering for that purpose — is genuinely unexpected and fortuitous.” Although the underlying physics of the effects remain unclear (an issue exacerbated by the fact that GlobalFoundries’s intellectual property restricts access to certain process details), this should not, he argues, delay the use of such devices in quantum computers.
